analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and locks in a 35% cap on gift taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote; it sat in the Finance Committee from January 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019, despite 38 Republican senators signing on and no Democratic support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the federal estate tax, which is levied on large fortunes passed to heirs after death, and repeal the related tax on generation-skipping transfers. It would keep the gift tax but cap its top rate at 35% and lock in a $5 million lifetime exemption with inflation adjustments. In practice, the estate tax already applies only to the largest estates, so repeal would be a large tax cut for a very small group of very wealthy families.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax only applies to fortunes above the exemption amount (roughly $5.5 million per person and about $11 million per couple in 2017, a threshold that applied to a tiny fraction of estates). Those families' heirs would pay nothing on the inherited fortune instead of a tax that can reach 40% on the amount above the exemption. Wealthy individuals could also pass wealth during life at a capped 35% gift tax rate with a permanent $5 million exemption.
analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The estate tax is a source of federal revenue paid by the largest estates; repeal would shrink revenue, meaning more federal borrowing or less spending elsewhere for everyone else.
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated on a small number of very wealthy families, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers. Because the tax already exempts the vast majority of estates, the bill delivers its gains to the top and is poorly designed as broad tax relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2019.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept collecting the estate tax, so ordinary taxpayers did not have to make up the cost of repeal; the wealthiest estates also saw no change.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 24, 2017 and led it as principal sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Signed on as a cosponsor of the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

for.name: 37 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of every one of its signers from a single party.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 24, 2017 and took no further action on it for the rest of the 115th Congress, so it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 37 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democrats attached to the bill; the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it, was chaired by a Republican, so it died without opposition ever having to vote.

industries.note: Repeal would erase the estate tax on inherited fortunes above the exemption threshold and cap lifetime gift taxes at 35%, a direct gain for the largest family fortunes. The cost is the lost federal revenue, which falls on taxpayers generally rather than on the families receiving the cut.

A permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes would shrink the need for the elaborate trusts and planning strategies built to avoid those taxes. The industry's interest runs against a tax cut it loses business from, though transition planning would create temporary work.
